title: CLO 2025 Course: Celebrate the Motherland's Anniversary by Creating National Day Themed Dresses with CLO
description:
The National Day themed dress live replay is here!  
Technical experts are online to teach you how to use the new 3D Pen (virtual model) feature in CLO 2025.1 to quickly design dress structures.  
Experts explain step-by-step to help you master the new features and speed up your workflow! Free resources are available on the CLO official WeChat account “CLO3D”; reply with “National Day” in the message box to receive them.
transcript:
Today, I will explain the production of a group of dresses with a National Day theme.

First, let's analyze the structure of the dress we are going to make. It consists of three-dimensional flame-shaped panels that surround the model's chest and the back of the head. We also need to create a folding structure like this, along with fishbone components and a three-dimensional double-layered umbrella sleeve. Additionally, there is a three-dimensional structure extending from the waist to the hips, plus a skirt.

In the materials provided, there are PNG images showing both the front and back views. These help us better understand the construction and represent the final effect of this production. The theme of this dress is National Day.

There are only two days, then one day left before the National Day holiday begins. I wish you an early happy holiday.

Now, let’s enter CLO.

First, we load our material folder into the library window. Then we import the model into CLO. This model’s size and proportions were adjusted based on the overall proportions and shape of the dress. It is relatively tall, with a slightly larger bust and hips, embodying a model with golden ratio proportions.

If you want to use other models, such as Naomi, you can directly use the AVS format virtual model size file in the Virtual Model Editor.

Next, we use our 3D pen. In the latest 2025.1 version, the 3D pen virtual model function has been improved. Previously, we could only draw the 3D pen on the virtual model to create flat panels. Now, we can create points in space.

First, we draw a midline on the model, which represents the waistline’s center. Then, we switch to the model’s side to draw a side seam line. Because the span is relatively large, we hold the Ctrl key to draw a waistline that fits the model’s body by left-clicking to draw straight line points. After finishing the line, we can also use the Edit 3D Pen function to modify the segments.

Since we need to draw the side seam, I deactivate and hide the model’s arms for easier operation.

Next, we draw a panel contour around the model’s chest. This dress has fishbone structures under the chest and waist, so we first draw a fishbone width of about 7 to 8 millimeters at the center point by double-clicking to finish the line. Then, holding Ctrl, we draw a complete closed circular line along the bottom of the chest to form the outline.

Using the Edit 3D Pen function, we fine-tune the outline to make the lines smooth and check from different angles.

We then draw a dividing line on the chest to help the chest panel fit the model’s chest better and adjust its curvature.

After adjusting the chest curve, look at the overall structure. This structure includes the fishbone and needs to be painted like a vest. Such a dress not only contains fishbone structures that support the waist and can bear heavier weight but also requires a transparent mesh structure on the shoulder to better support the whole dress. This can be done in CLO, and the appearance looks like a chest piece.

We draw the chest curve and then the back seam line, including the back waistline. Adding points here helps make the connections smoother.

Since we are using the 3D pen function, the drawing process might take longer, around half an hour or more.

Next, we draw the neckline, which is made with transparent mesh. Then we draw the armhole section and proceed downward. The back piece has a strapless effect, so we drag and align it smoothly, adding curve points to make the transition seamless.

This completes the general upper body structure.

Next, we begin drawing the fishbone, which is divided into three equal parts. We pay attention to the proportions to ensure they are aesthetically pleasing. We draw three dividing lines on the front, corresponding to a four-part division, and fine-tune the visual three-part ratio. The front has its own side waistline, making the waist appear slimmer and enhancing the body proportions.

Then we draw the back piece divisions, maintaining the three-part ratio based on the front for visual harmony.

Next, we draw the shoulder dividing lines following the same method.

Now, to add points in space, we first add points on the model by default. Pressing the P key creates points in space. When creating a point in space, we can press the left mouse button to place it. Holding Ctrl while creating points allows us to draw curves. We constantly rotate the model left and right to check and adjust the positions of points, which requires spatial awareness.

Continuing, we draw the side seam line on the hip, adjusting the position with the curve tool. We then draw the back piece in space using the P key and Ctrl to curve the line, noting the color-coded axis lines in the interface to gauge distances and positions.

We can switch points between the model surface and space by pressing the P key.

Next, we draw sound lines (seam lines) on the front and back with the left mouse button, ending with a double click.

Using the flat surface tool, lines showing blue indicate selectable panels for flat surface creation. After selecting the area, pressing Enter creates the flat surface.

We select multiple panels by holding Shift, then press Enter to flatten them all simultaneously, establishing sewing relationships and simplifying the sewing process. We flatten front and back panels separately but need to pay attention to sewing lines.

Next, we adjust lines such as the neckline arcs using the Edit 3D Pen tool, changing some straight lines to curves and optimizing points to reduce their number.

We then freeze the panels and sew them using 1-to-n sewing with the Shift key to facilitate the process.

After sewing, we simulate the garment. If the chest side seems unstable when showing translucency, we harden the chest pad to make it firmer and better adhere to the model’s chest, a common trick for making underwear.

We then pinch and harden the bottom plates, lifting the outfit upon simulation.

Next, we add fabrics from the material window, applying silk fabrics to the clothing panels and transparent ebony fabric to hollow waist panels.

Now, we create the bottom fish tail skirt structure. Using a round plate with a diameter of 22 mm, we create a hole in the middle representing the knee circumference. We draw a cross with internal basic lines to position it and calculate the circumference.

The external line is 700 mm downward from the knee to the ground, which is the skirt length.

After positioning, we sew the pieces and simulate. The circular shape is large; we merge front panels and connect fishbone structures symmetrically.

We adjust lengths, convert points to curves, and optimize curves to reduce points and ensure smoothness.

Next, we use the 3D pen function to draw flame-shaped panels extending from the collar to the chest and the back of the head. We carefully place each point on the garment surface, avoiding large gaps to prevent points from embedding inside panels or the garment.

We adjust the lines’ curvature and direction, drawing from the chest to the waist and hips, pressing Ctrl to curve and double-clicking to finish lines.

After completing the flame shapes, we draw smaller flame details, creating points in space and adjusting shapes with the 3D pen tool for better aesthetics.

We close the shape, smooth the collar, and attempt to flatten the panels. If flattening fails due to problematic lines (indicated by red), we edit the 3D pen lines, deleting excess lines, and try flattening again.

We adjust the panels’ arcs and shapes, converting straight lines to curves and optimizing points to reduce their number.

Next, we create curved plates based on lengths needed to support the desired shape during simulation. These plates are frozen (locked) to prevent deformation and sewn separately.

We apply hardening to these support plates before simulation to maintain the three-dimensional shape, similar to iron wires or stiff materials like fishbone in real dresses.

We add fixed pins (fake sewing needles) to the front chest to prevent deformation during simulation. After natural simulation, we adjust and freeze shapes, deleting fixed pins afterward.

We sew the chest’s two main panels onto the garment. Before sewing, we freeze large plates and add internal lines using the 3D pen tool. We hide the virtual model during this process for clarity.

By right-clicking, we unlock joints and delete unnecessary internal lines to avoid interference.

We sew all parts in sequence using 1-to-n sewing with Shift key, ensuring the seams are properly closed. After sewing, we simulate to check the structure.

If there are small holes or overlaps, we adjust points slightly to improve fit.

Next, we draw folds on three-dimensional panels using the inner line tool, making lines about 10 mm apart for evenness. We use the fold-over folding tool to select and adjust fold strength and rendering.

We manually adjust fold positions for a more natural look, ensuring edges align with panel borders.

Then, we support the three-dimensional shape to allow movement for posing, walking, animation, etc. We fix fake sewing needles to the virtual model, measuring positions and lengths, and entering values carefully.

After fixing these supports, we simulate and adjust positions for smoothness.

We add lines and folds to create fuller shapes and more beautiful waves on the fabric.

We adjust folding strength and positions, ensuring the folds are not too tight.

Next, we create sleeves and front skirt parts using the 3D pen virtual model. We create points in space along desired curves, drawing upper and lower edges of the sleeve, adjusting curves, and sewing the sleeve edges with the garment.

We also sew collarbone areas and back parts similarly.

We adjust curve lines on the sleeves because the bottom is wider than the top, pulling curves for a smooth transition.

Using the 3D pen tool, we hook internal lines, untie chains, delete unnecessary lines, and hook outer and inner lines to finalize shapes.

We delete the 3D pen lines that interfere, then create new points wider than the original outline to add fold effects, drawing square or coin-shaped panels with smooth arcs.

After flattening and optimizing curves, we draw and cut lines on the upper edge and create a middle line, then drag panels out and freeze all clothes.

We reactivate the bottom skirt and sew it, folding and hardening before sewing.

Using 1-to-n sewing, we attach panels carefully and simulate.

If needed, we adjust particle diameter, fold strength, and fold positions.

We copy fold boards to increase volume and sew them, making folds more natural.

We draw rectangular panels for the skirt’s bottom, set width and height, rotate, and sew onto lines. We freeze panels to prevent penetration and adjust volume by pulling out folds and rounding corners.

We redo the 2D arrangement for better remodeling and smooth arcs.

We copy smaller panels to sew onto fold panels and paste internal lines on them, adjusting arcs for smooth seam connections without cold corners.

We simulate and adjust for any penetration issues.

Using the sewing tool, we add small fold lines on desired positions, similar to lines made on real silk garments.

We add sewing needles at the right positions, tuck folds, pull and adjust fold states, and delete sewing needles before simulating again for natural effects.

We push fold templates inside slightly for more natural folds.

Next, we apply fabrics from the material bag: silk and semi-transparent ebony. We apply silk to all clothing panels and ebony to hollow waist panels.

We increase the thickness of ebony fabric to about 3.5 for better effect, then simulate.

The fabric materials create layered effects.

We then create positioning prints by exporting 2D quick photos, editing in Photoshop to add flame-shaped patterns with black and orange-yellow brushes to simulate burning effects on edges.

We build new layers, adjust opacity to 20-30%, and use soft-edged brushes to apply the effect, emphasizing the design concept of stars’ fire having a healing effect.

We export the edited PNG images and save as our original style.

For sleeves, we add hard flowers made in advance with dark black colors at the top to keep the flame shape distinct and prevent the appearance from being too messy.

We add decorative threads from the material bag, including gem-shaped and basic threads, especially on fishbone edges.

We arrange thread rhythms, colors, and materials creatively to fit the design.

After adding all decorations, we change the model’s pose and freeze and hide decoration strips.

We fix any holes at corners using the grid tool, hardening penetrating areas to improve appearance.

After freezing, we simulate again and check the overall effect.

If holes appear on the back, we untie frozen boards, simulate, adjust overall state, and freeze again.

Finally, we improve quality, simulate, and set the model’s skin texture to one without underwear to avoid showing beneath the dress.

Lighting files (HDRI environment pictures) are provided in the material bag for better rendering.

You can choose your preferred angle for presentation.

This concludes today’s live content.

chunks.content: ## Overview of National Day Themed Dress Production in CLO 2025 This section introduces the design concept and structural components of a National Day themed dress created using CLO 2025. Key elements include three-dimensional flame-shaped panels, fishbone support structures, double-layered umbrella sleeves, and a skirt with a structured waist-to-hip extension. --- ## Dress Structure and Design Components The dress features several distinctive three-dimensional elements: - Flame-shaped panels surrounding the chest and back of the head. - A folding structure integrated with fishbone components. - A double-layered umbrella sleeve. - A three-dimensional structure extending from the waist to the hips. - A fish tail bottom skirt. PNG images of front and back views assist in visualizing the final product. The design theme aligns with National Day celebrations, emphasizing symbolic fire/flame motifs. --- ## Initial Model Setup and Material Import in CLO - Load material folder into CLO’s library. - Import the virtual model with proportions adjusted for height, bust, and hips reflecting golden ratio proportions. - Alternative models (e.g., Naomi) can be imported via AVS format files using the Virtual Model Editor. --- ## Using the 3D Pen Tool in CLO 2025.1 The 3D Pen tool has enhanced capabilities: - Ability to create points in 3D space, not just on model surfaces. - Drawing midlines (waist center), side seams, and panel outlines with precision. - Holding Ctrl enables drawing straight or curved lines with point placement. - The Edit 3D Pen function allows fine-tuning of points and smooth curvature adjustments. For ease of drawing side seams, model arms can be hidden. --- ## Drawing and Refining the Dress Panels - Draw fishbone structures beneath the chest and waist with widths around 7-8 mm. - Outline chest panels with closed circular lines, adjusting curvature for a better fit. - Draw dividing lines on chest and back for structural support and sewing guides. - Fishbone components support heavier weight; transparent mesh on shoulders provides additional support. - Neckline and armhole are drawn with transparent mesh, with back strapless designs smoothly curved. - Drawing major structural lines with 3D Pen can take 30+ minutes. --- ## Fishbone and Panel Division Proportions - Fishbone divided into three equal parts for aesthetic balance. - Front panels divided into four parts visually approximated to three. - Side waistlines enhance body proportion perception. - Back piece and shoulder lines maintain symmetrical three-part ratios. --- ## Creating Points in 3D Space and Seam Lines - Pressing P key enables adding points in space; left-click places points. - Holding Ctrl while adding points allows curve creation. - Points can be toggled between surface and space modes with the P key. - Seam lines (sound lines) are drawn on front and back panels, finalized by double-click. - Flat surface tool identifies selectable panels (blue lines) for flattening. - Multiple panels can be selected with Shift and flattened simultaneously. - Sewing relationships are established between panels post-flattening.
